title: Black Tie Optional Wedding Guest Dresses
metaTitle: Black Tie Optional Wedding Guest Dresses: The Rules, Decoded
metaDescription: Black tie optional wedding guest dresses explained: what the Emily Post Institute allows, which fabrics and hem lengths read formal, and the questions guests ask most.
h1: Black Tie Optional Wedding Guest Dresses: What the Code Actually Obliges You To
intro: Black tie optional wedding guest dresses run from a floor-length evening gown down to a dressy cocktail dress, and the Emily Post Institute also accepts a little black dress or dressy separates. What the code rules out is daywear: anything you would wear to the office or to a casual party. Length gives you room to choose; fabric is where most guests go wrong.
answer: For black tie optional, wear a floor-length evening gown, a dressy cocktail dress, a little black dress or dressy separates, which is the Emily Post Institute's list. A midi or knee-length dress is fine if the fabric is formal: satin, velvet, silk crepe, heavy georgette or sequins. Skip cotton, linen, jersey and anything that reads as daywear.

contentSections.heading: What the code allows, and where the line is
contentSections.content:
The Emily Post Institute's attire guide gives women four options for black tie optional: a formal floor-length evening gown, a dressy cocktail dress, a little black dress, or dressy separates. Compare that with full black tie, which lists a floor-length gown, a dressy cocktail dress, or your dressiest little black dress. The difference is small. Optional adds dressy separates and relaxes the little black dress from your dressiest to simply a good one. The word optional is mostly about the men, for whom a dark suit becomes acceptable in place of a tuxedo.

So a midi or a knee-length dress is not a compromise here; it is on the list, as long as it is a dressy cocktail dress. The test is whether the dress would look at home at an evening party in a hotel ballroom. A matte cotton shift would not; the same cut in duchess satin would.

Read the start time too. Emily Post advises erring toward formality for semi-formal events after 6 p.m., and the same logic applies here: a six o'clock ceremony followed by dinner and dancing rewards a longer hem and a more formal fabric than a two o'clock ceremony with the same wording. At a daytime black tie optional wedding, a tea-length or midi dress with some sheen is right at home.

contentSections.heading: Choose a fabric that reads formal at night
contentSections.content:
Velvet absorbs light instead of reflecting it, so it looks rich under warm reception lighting and flat at a midday ceremony. Keep it for evening weddings from autumn through winter.

Silk crepe and heavy triple georgette are among the safest choices. They have enough weight to hang straight, they do not crease badly across the lap during a seated dinner, and they photograph as a clean block of color.

Duchess satin is beautiful and unforgiving. It throws a hard band of light along every curve, and a camera flash can blow that band out to white. If you love satin, a matte-face satin is easier to wear.

Chiffon needs a good lining. Unlined chiffon over a nude slip can turn semi-transparent under uplighting. Sequins are welcome at this code, provided they are stitched rather than glued and the base fabric is heavy enough to carry their weight without sagging off the shoulder.

contentSections.heading: Where should the hem fall?
contentSections.content:
Floor-length: aim for the hem to sit about half an inch off the floor in the shoes you will actually wear. A hem that pools gets stepped on by the third dance.

Midi: placement matters more than the label. The best point is the narrowest part of the calf, usually mid-calf or just below. A hem that stops at the widest part of the calf shortens the leg in photographs.

Tea-length, just above the ankle bone, is an underused option and an especially good one for a daytime version of this code.

Knee-length works when the dress is clearly a cocktail dress: a formal fabric, a defined shape, evening shoes. Above the knee is the length most likely to feel underdressed at an evening reception.

contentSections.heading: Check the construction before you commit
contentSections.content:
A formal dress shows its quality from a distance. Look at the lining first: it should run to the hem in something smooth, not stop at the hip. An exposed plastic zipper up the back of an otherwise formal dress is visible in every photo taken from behind. Boning that ripples through the fabric when you sit will ripple all evening. And be wary of anything sold as formal that weighs almost nothing; a gown that folds down to the size of a paperback will hang like a nightgown.

If the dress needs altering, allow time. Shortening a lined formal dress means shortening the lining separately, and taking in a boned bodice means opening it up. Book the tailor before you order, and work backward to your order date.

faqs.question: Can I wear black to a black tie optional wedding?
faqs.answer: Yes. The little black dress is on Emily Post's list for this code. Head-to-toe flat black can photograph as a silhouette with no detail, so break it up with a textured fabric such as velvet or lace, a metallic shoe or a strong earring.

faqs.question: Does a jumpsuit count?
faqs.answer: Yes, as dressy separates or an evening alternative, if the tailoring is serious: a crepe or satin jumpsuit with a proper waist seam and a lined bodice. A soft jersey jumpsuit reads as loungewear under bright light.

faqs.question: If the wedding is in the evening, do I have to wear floor-length?
faqs.answer: No. A dressy cocktail dress is on the list at any hour. If you would rather not think about it during the speeches, a floor-length dress removes the question; otherwise make sure the fabric is doing the work.

faqs.question: Can I wear a print?
faqs.answer: Yes, if the scale is right. Large, painterly florals and abstract prints on a dark ground hold their formality. Small, busy repeats such as ditsy florals, fine polka dots and thin stripes read casual from across a room and can shimmer on camera.

faqs.question: What shoes work for black tie optional?
faqs.answer: A closed or nearly closed toe in satin, suede or metallic leather. Check the ground first: grass, gravel, cobbles or an old terrace will swallow a stiletto. A block heel of two to three inches looks just as formal and lasts the night.

faqs.question: Which colors should I avoid?
faqs.answer: White, ivory, cream, champagne, and anything that photographs as white under a flash, such as very pale blush, oyster and the palest silver. Beyond that, avoid matching the bridal party if you know its colors.
